Cohorts and subsets

Source: vignettes/cohorts-and-subsets.Rmd
cohorts-and-subsets.Rmd
library(plasgenomicsutilsR)
ps <- example_pop_structure(umap = FALSE)

Most analyses here are run on some subset of a callset – one region, the monoclonal infections, everything except a sample that turned out to be a duplicate. This article is about getting that subset right, because two of the ways it can go wrong are silent.

Narrowing a PopStructure

$subset() takes sample ids, metadata filters, or both:

ps$subset(country = "Ghana")
#> <PopStructure> 30 of 60 samples, 49 PCs
#>   UMAP: -   sNMF: -   meta: country
ps$subset(samples = ps$get_samples()[1:10])
#> <PopStructure> 10 of 60 samples, 49 PCs
#>   UMAP: -   sNMF: -   meta: country

drop_samples removes named samples after the other filters, so a sample can be taken out even though the filter it sits inside keeps it – a contaminant or a duplicate, without having to spell out the whole keep list:

ps$subset(country = "Ghana", drop_samples = ps$get_samples()[1])
#> <PopStructure> 30 of 60 samples, 49 PCs
#>   UMAP: -   sNMF: -   meta: country

Ids that are not in the object are named in a warning rather than passed over, since a typo otherwise looks exactly like a sample that had already gone.

A subset refits on itself

PCA, UMAP and sNMF are joint fits: where a sample lands depends on which other samples were in the fit. So a refit after subsetting is fit on the subset alone, not on the whole cohort with the extra rows filtered out afterwards.

sub <- ps$subset(country = "Ghana")
sub$run_umap(pca_components = 5)
c(cohort = length(ps$get_samples()), subset = nrow(sub$umap_df()))
#> cohort subset 
#>     60     30

That matters when a sample looks like an outlier: it may only be one by reference to samples you have since excluded. Re-running the embedding on the retained cohort is the check.

The object subsetted from is untouched, so the two can be compared.

Metadata column names

sample, Sample and SAMPLE are the same column to everyone except a string comparison, and metadata arrives from whoever assembled it. Any capitalisation is accepted, wherever a meta table is taken:

caps <- data.frame(Sample = ps$get_samples(), site = rep(c("a", "b"), length.out = 60))
names(ps$subset(samples = ps$get_samples())$get_meta())
#> [1] "sample"  "country"
head(names(PopStructure$new(ps$genotype(), meta = caps)$get_meta()), 3)
#> reading metadata column `Sample` as `sample`
#> [1] "sample" "site"

An exact sample wins outright, so a table holding both sample and Sample is not ambiguous; two non-exact variants is an error, since which one holds the ids is not the package’s to guess.

The scans run on the cohort parasite_haplotypes() kept. A diversity or differentiation

estimate that is meant to describe those same parasites has to be given the same set – otherwise the paper says “monoclonal infections” while the table was computed over everything. haplotype_samples() is that set. The example callset carries no Fws, so here is an illustrative one to gate on:

set.seed(1)
fws <- data.frame(sample = rownames(ps$genotype()),
                  fws = stats::runif(nrow(ps$genotype()), 0.80, 1))
gated <- parasite_haplotypes(ps, fws = fws, min_fws = 0.95, maf = 0.05)

mono <- haplotype_samples(gated)
c(genotyped = nrow(ps$genotype()), in_haplotypes = length(mono))
#>     genotyped in_haplotypes 
#>            60            14

It is what survived every filter, not only the Fws gate: samples left too incomplete by max_sample_missing are gone too. gated$filtering says how many went to each cause, which is worth a glance before quoting a sample count.

gated$filtering[c("n_dropped_polyclonal", "n_dropped_sample_missing")]
#> $n_dropped_polyclonal
#> [1] 46
#> 
#> $n_dropped_sample_missing
#> [1] 0

subset_genotypes() narrows a panel to them, and gives back the same kind of object it was handed – a load_genotypes() list stays a list, with sample.id moved to match:

pop_diversity(subset_genotypes(ps, gated), group = "country",
              accessible = PF3D7_CORE_REGIONS)[, c("group", "n_samples", "pi", "n_hap")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   group    n_samples         pi n_hap
#>   <fct>        <int>      <dbl> <int>
#> 1 Cambodia         8 0.00000140     8
#> 2 Ghana            6 0.00000709     6

against the ungated cohort:

pop_diversity(ps, group = "country",
              accessible = PF3D7_CORE_REGIONS)[, c("group", "n_samples", "pi", "n_hap")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   group    n_samples         pi n_hap
#>   <fct>        <int>      <dbl> <int>
#> 1 Cambodia        30 0.00000185    26
#> 2 Ghana           30 0.00000707    30

Two things this is deliberately not doing. It subsets samples and keeps every SNP, because a diversity estimate wants the whole panel; hap$hap is MAF-filtered and imputed to the 0/1 matrix needs, so handing that to pop_diversity() would quietly answer a different question. And metadata needs no subsetting – it is matched by sample, so extra rows are ignored.

The columns that most need this are n_hap and hap_div: counting distinct haplotypes across SNP combinations only means something when each sample is one genome. pi, he and seg_sites still read on mixed infections, they just describe a cohort you did not describe in the methods.
